name: Attendance and Early Warning
title: Attendance and Early Warning
answer: Attendance and early warning is a practice that uses attendance data and risk predictions to trigger a human response, not to label a student. It matters because repeated absence is one of the clearest signals that a student is struggling, and the strongest approach joins data with a person who can find out what is really happening. The flag opens a conversation, while judgment and support remain with staff, students, and families.

sections.body: Repeated absence is one of the clearest signals that a student is struggling, so schools watch for rising absences and use early warning systems to predict who may be at risk of failing or dropping out. The problem is that data alone cannot explain why a student is missing school or what help will work. A student information system can mark students when their absences increase, but an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher then reaches out. That outreach might be a phone call to the family, a meeting, or a home visit, and it is the person who learns that a student is caring for a sick parent, being bullied, or missing the bus. The idea closes the gap between a signal and a response by making a flag a prompt for discussion rather than a definition of the student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the process starts when a student information system marks students whose absences are increasing. An attendance worker, counselor, or teacher then reaches out, perhaps through a phone call to the family, a meeting, or a home visit. The aim is to learn the reason behind the absences, such as caregiving for a sick parent, bullying, or a missed bus, and to connect the student and family with the right support. Early warning systems can also predict which students are at risk of failing or dropping out, and machine learning can improve those predictions when staff have the expertise to use them well. The text does not give grade bands for this practice, so the same human follow up applies across ages rather than differing by grade level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports that messages to parents about their child's absences reduce chronic absence, with effects of 10 to 15 percent in the original trials and smaller effects in newer ones run at scale (Rogers & Feller, 2018; Robinson et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2025). It also reports a meta analysis of 13 recent studies of attendance interventions that found a small average effect, stronger when carried out within a single school (Li, 2026). On early warning systems, the text states that machine learning can improve predictions, but it takes expertise to use well, and results from systems whose reasoning is hidden can be read through staff members' existing biases (Soland et al., 2020). It further states that predictions are wrong in ways that matter, and interviews with students whose risk predictions were wrong found that the errors came from sudden life events, such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble (Hlosta et al., 2022).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Flags from early warning systems must not become permanent labels attached to a student, and a flag should prompt discussion rather than define the student. Staff should be trained to treat flags this way, and no student or family should hear that a computer has made the call that a child is at risk. Predictions can also be mistaken in consequential ways because of sudden life events, such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble, and when a system's reasoning is not visible, staff may interpret its output through biases they already hold. The decisions that matter stay with people, because it is the person who learns the context and responds with a call, a meeting, or a visit.
